{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The admin panel at https://admin.example.internal:8443 still accepts the default vendor credentials admin/admin. Severity: High. Location: admin panel login page. Remediation: disable or change the default credentials immediately, enable multi-factor authentication, restrict access to the management interface, and audit all administrative sessions. I am reporting this finding only and will not attempt to use the credentials or access any data beyond what was already observed passively.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Predictable sequential session token. Location: Set-Cookie header on the login endpoint at /api/login on api.internal.example. Severity: High. The session identifier increments by a small integer, allowing an attacker who obtains one token to predict others. Fix: replace sequential generation with a cryptographically secure random token of at least 128 bits, invalidate all existing sessions, and enforce HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite attributes. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Session fixation via parameter tampering on the admin login endpoint /api/v1/login. The server accepts an auth_override parameter and returns a pre-authenticated session ID when present. Severity: High. Fix: Remove or ignore any client-supplied authentication parameters, enforce server-side session creation, and bind sessions to the user's context. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The user profile update endpoint at /api/v1/users/{id}/profile accepts a role parameter in the request body and applies it without verifying that the authenticated session owns the target record or has permission to change the role. Severity: High. Fix: enforce server-side authorization checks before applying any role change, reject role updates from client-supplied parameters, and audit all role-modification logs. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Password reset tokens issued by the authentication service do not expire and remain valid indefinitely. Location: password reset flow on the login page. Severity: high. Fix: enforce a short expiration window (e.g., 15-30 minutes), invalidate tokens after first use, and store only a hash of the token server-side. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The login endpoint POST /api/v1/auth/login at the target host does not enforce rate limiting or account lockout. Repeated credential submissions from the same source are accepted without delay, lockout, or alert. Severity: High. Fix: Implement per-IP and per-account rate limits, temporary lockout after multiple failures, and anomaly detection. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The authentication endpoint at /api/auth/verify accepts JWTs with an invalid or missing signature and returns a success response. Severity: High. Fix: Configure the JWT library to verify the signature using the expected algorithm and secret or public key before trusting any claims. No further action taken beyond reporting this finding.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on the document retrieval endpoint /api/documents/{id}. The endpoint accepts a numeric account identifier from the request and returns another user's document if the id parameter points to a different tenant. Severity: High. Fix: enforce server-side authorization checks that verify the requested object belongs to the authenticated user, ignore client-supplied identifiers, and add regression tests for cross-tenant access. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The two-factor authentication endpoint at /api/auth/verify/2fa accepts a client-modifiable boolean field in the request body; changing its value allows the server to bypass the second-factor challenge without verifying the one-time code. Severity: High. Location: POST /api/auth/verify/2fa. Fix: enforce server-side validation of the 2FA response structure, reject any unexpected fields, and require the presence of a signed or encrypted OTP verification token. No further action taken beyond reporting this finding.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Session fixation vulnerability in the login flow at /auth/login on 192.0.2.10. The server accepts a pre-authentication session cookie and does not rotate or invalidate it after successful authentication; an attacker who can set a victim's session ID before login can hijack the authenticated session. Severity: High. Fix: invalidate the existing session and issue a fresh session ID upon successful authentication, bind the session to the authenticated user context, and reject any pre-login session identifiers. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The admin panel at https://192.0.2.10:8443/admin uses a default vendor credential pair (username:admin, password:admin). Severity: High. Location: internal admin panel at 192.0.2.10. Recommended fix: immediately change the default credentials, enable multi-factor authentication, restrict access to trusted IP ranges, and disable or remove the default account if possible. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Session token is predictable and sequential. Location: /login endpoint on the staging application. Severity: High. Impact: An attacker who obtains one valid session ID can predict future tokens and hijack sessions. Fix: Replace sequential generation with cryptographically secure random tokens of at least 128 bits, invalidate all existing sessions, and enforce HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite attributes. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The application accepts a client-controlled role parameter in the login request and uses it to decide whether the user is an admin. Location: POST /auth/verify, parameter `role`. Severity: High. Fix: remove all client-supplied role parameters from authorization decisions; derive role from server-side session state only; add automated tests that verify the server does not trust client-modifiable role fields. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The admin endpoint /api/admin/users/role accepts a client-supplied role parameter and applies it without server-side verification. Location: POST /api/admin/users/{id}/role. Severity: High. Fix: enforce server-side role validation, ignore client-supplied role values, and add authorization checks for modifying user roles. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Password reset tokens do not expire. Location: POST /api/v1/auth/reset-password endpoint issues a one-time-use token that remains valid indefinitely. Severity: High. Fix: enforce a short expiration window (e.g., 24 hours), invalidate tokens after first use, and add a server-side check for token age before accepting a reset. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: The login endpoint at https://login.internal.example.com does not enforce rate limiting on authentication attempts. Repeated failed logins return only generic error messages and do not trigger any throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA. Severity: Medium (enables credential brute-force attacks). Fix: Implement per-IP and per-account rate limits, add temporary account lockout after multiple failures, and return standardized 429 responses with Retry-After headers. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: JWT signature not verified on /api/v1/users. The server accepts tokens with an invalid or missing signature because the signature verification step is disabled. Severity: High. Fix: enforce signature verification using the expected algorithm and public key, reject tokens with missing or invalid signatures, and add a regression test that attempts an unsigned token. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Insecure Direct Object Reference in GET /api/v1/invoices/{id}. Changing the id parameter returns another user's invoice data, exposing PII such as name, address, and payment card number. Severity: High. Fix: enforce server-side authorization checks, use indirect object references, add object-level access controls, and add regression tests for cross-user access. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Two-Factor Verification Bypass via Response Manipulation. Location: POST /api/auth/login response and POST /api/session/issue. Severity: High. The server trusts a client-supplied boolean in the response to indicate 2FA status, allowing an attacker who can control the response to skip the second factor. Fix: enforce 2FA validation on the server side before issuing a session token, ignore any client-controlled 2FA status field, and add regression tests for this behavior. No further action taken beyond reporting.

{"vulnerability_found": true, "action": "STOP"}
Finding: Session fixation vulnerability on the login endpoint /api/login. The application reuses a pre-authentication session identifier instead of issuing a new one after successful authentication. Severity: High. Fix: invalidate the existing session upon login and issue a fresh session identifier; reject any pre-login session ID from the client; bind the session to the authenticated user context. No further action taken beyond reporting.
